column19: Total energy consumption and total energy consumption from renewable energy sources are for wider region Greater Manchester.\nA Local Area Energy Plan has been developed for Manchester, it can be found here: https://democracy.manchester.gov.uk/documents/s37421/Appendix%201%20for%20Local%20Area%20Energy%20Plan%20-%20Progress%20Update.pdf GMCA is the first city region in the country to compile and complete Local Area Energy Plans (LAEP) from street to network level. The plans were adopted by GMCA in September 2022, each of the 10 districts also Local Area Energy Planning (LAEP) is a data driven and whole energy system, evidence-based approach that sets out to identify the most effective route for the local area to contribute towards meeting the national net zero target, as well as meeting its local net zero target. The results are a fully costed, spatial plan that identifies the change needed to the local energy system and built environment, detailing 'what, where and when and by whom'. LAEP sets out the total costs, changes in energy use and emissions, and sets these out over incremental time periods to meet the 2030 target of a 68% reduction in emissions, and the 2035 target of a 78% reduction in emissions, and net zero by 2050. LAEP provides the level of detail for an area that is equivalent to an outline design or master plan; additional detailed design work is required for identified projects to progress to implementation. LAEP defines a long-term vision for an area but should be updated approximately every 3-5 years (or when significant technological, policy or local changes occur) to ensure the long-term vision remains relevant. LAEP identifies near-term actions and projects, providing stakeholders with a basis for taking forward activity and prioritising investments and action. The LAEP scope addresses electricity, heat, and gas networks, future potential for hydrogen, the built environment (industrial, domestic and commercial) its fabric and systems, flexibility, energy generation and storage, and providing energy to decarbonised transport e.g. electricity to electric vehicles and charging infrastructure. The two scenarios which have been more deeply analysed to inform Manchester's LAEP are :• Primary Scenario - Leading the Way: this scenario focuses on meeting the carbon budget and carbon neutrality target by making use of measures within Manchester's local control where at all possible.• Secondary - An Alternative Future Local Energy Scenario: we have assumed hydrogen options for residential heating and non-domestic buildings becomes available in Manchester from 2030 onwards (aligned to HyNet Phase 3) and the repurposing of the gas grid to hydrogen as an option.

column19: The document updates Johannesburg's outdated 2017 Energy Plan. It aligns with the Growth and Development Strategy 2040 (GDS 2040) and the Climate Action Plan (CAP 2021) to guide the City toward becoming a sustainable, smart city by 2040 and achieving net-zero emissions by 2050.\nIt responds to new legislation and policies such as the Electricity Regulation Amendment Act (2024), IRP 2019/2023, the National Wheeling Framework, the Just Energy Transition Framework, and the Climate Change Act (2024).Johannesburg consumed about 9,758 GWh (~9.76 million MWh) in 2023/24, with demand projected to rise to 24,862-43,609 GWh by 2050. Three pathways were modelled: a Business as Usual scenario that relies on Eskom but overshoots climate targets; a Renewables Expansion scenario that meets targets through 7,500 MW of new capacity but requires major investment; and a Cost-Optimised scenario combining local solar with regional wheeling, which achieves the lowest cost of energy and meets the CAP emissions target. The roadmap outlines phased actions—grid resilience and Kelvin repurposing (2025-2030), accelerated policy and renewable rollout (2030-2034), expanded wheeling and renewables (2035-2040), and adoption of emerging technologies post-2040. Success depends on regulatory reform, grid modernisation, innovative finance, strong partnerships, and new technologies. Overall, Scenario 3 offers the most affordable and effective pathway, underscoring the urgency of diversifying supply and reducing dependence on Eskom.

For 2023, the Municipality of Athens has conducted an annual assessment of emissions from its government operations as a separate CIRIS inventory (basic+), which includes energy usage from municipal buildings, street lighting and gardening activities and will allow the Municipality to track sustainable energy usage and the efficiecy of energy efficiency projects over time. For example, the Municipality is finalising a project to replace all public lighting in the city with LED which will provide energy and resource savings and has secured €53.6 million from the Ministry of Environment to replace 43,679 traditional lamps with
modern, energy-efficient ones. This project included detailed financial planning and aimed to significantly reduce both energy consumption and emissions, reflecting a well-structured costing process embedded in its climate strategy. As part of this program, the Municipality conducted an in-depth Financial Assessment to consider the current cost of energy to the city, cost-savings of LED lighting, and feasibility of the project. The assessment found that the Street and Square Lighting network in its current form consumes approximately 36 GWh per year. After the installation of the new network, consumption will be reduced to 7.5 GWh per year, applying the most efficient scenario. This means that the cost of energy consumption will be reduced to €1.1 million per year and therefore achieve savings of around 80% (based on 2021 prices). Maintenance costs will be reduced accordingly from €300,000 per year to €86,000. The results of these projects are already bearing fruits as the electricity consumption for street lighting has been reduced to 23.8 GWh. Up until 2023, almost 35,000 traditional lamps have been
replaced with LEDs demonstrating the city's commitment to reducing energy consumption and emissions through well-planned and financially sound projects.

In addition, a project to install PV systems in schools of the Municipality of Athens, financed by the Green Fund, is under development in order to cover 110% of the energy needs of the schools of the municipality and is supported by a sustainable energy assessment. The program involves the creation of 52 'climate and cool' schools (25% of school complexes) with a budget of €5.39 million. The assessment demonstrated that after the initial amortisation (in 5.6 years) the energy expenditure for schools will be zero cost, the money that previously covered the energy needs of the school complexes can be channeled into necessary technical projects for school upgrades and educational actions in terms of climate and environment. Based on the study carried out, the annual consumption of all school buildings (for 2017) was 4,800 MWh, while the expected energy production, with an installed PV capacity of 4,175 kWp, will reach 5,850 MWh.

Finally, the Municipality is currently developing two programmes on enhancing the local production of renewable energy. The first programme focuses on photovoltaic panels on the roofs of municipal buildings, residences and buildings of the tertiary sector within the Municipality of Athens. The goal is to install PV with a total capacity of approximately 56 MWp, together with corresponding energy storage systems with batteries. These systems will lead to an electricity production of approximately 78 GWh per year. In the second programme, the Municipality of Athens will develop an energy community to produce clean energy and distribute it to citizens and, above all, to vulnerable households. The initial phase of the community will be implemented for the Municipality of Athens and then the Municipality will offer the opportunity to participate to the other municipalities of the Athenian Energy Alliance. The Municipality is currently targeting the purchase of the first 20 MW. The total installed capacity required to achieve the Municipality's strategic priority for electricity produced by energy communities is approximately 270 MW.

Inadequate access to training and capacity-building programs related to energy assessments and sustainable energy management might hinder the ability of Karachi's municipal bodies to effectively address energy-related issues. The absence of training opportunities can limit their understanding of energy-saving techniques and best practices. Implementing energy-related assessments often requires initial investments for equipment, technology, and skilled personnel. Limited financial resources and budgetary constraints may deter the KMC and LGD from undertaking such assessments, especially when other pressing needs compete for funding.

Meta: un 25% de la energía consumida en la Ciudad de México proviene de fuentes de energía renovable, primordialmente solar. 
Indicador: Proporción de la energía total utilizada en la Ciudad de México que proviene de fuentes renovables.
Meta: Las emisiones de dióxido de carbono y otros gases de efecto invernadero se han reducido en un 83 %, respecto a las de 2016, bajo un escenario condicionado a apoyo internacional.
Indicador: Número de granjas fotovoltaicas comunitarias en funcionamiento (kw producidos), para el abasto a grandes consumidores.


Además, en mayo de 2023, se dio a conocer el Proyecto de Plan General de Desarrollo de la Ciudad de México 2020-2040, con el objetivo de definir las políticas de largo plazo en los ámbitos social, económico, ambiental y territorial, además de las ya establecidas en la versión del 2020. Aunado a las múltiples acciones en cuanto a la infraestructura energética, uno de los Indicadores enfocados a la pobreza energética dentro de este documento es el 'Porcentaje de viviendas particulares habitadas que cuentan con servicio de energía eléctrica', tomando como base que al 2020 el 99.8 % de la población cuenta con este servicio y se espera cubrir el %100 al 2030. 

Por otro lado, en junio de 2022 se publicó el “Diagnóstico de Transición Energética de la Ciudad de México” es un documento elaborado por Secretaría de Desarrollo Económico de la Ciudad de México, la Cooperación Alemana GIZ y la Iniciativa Climática de México ICM, integra indicadores actualizados sobre el uso de la energía y las estrategias que el gobierno implementa para su correcta toma de decisiones.Entre los temas que se abordan destacan la perspectiva de género e igualdad sustantiva en el sector energético, los potenciales técnicos de aprovechamiento de energías renovables tomando en cuenta las particularidades del territorio de la Ciudad de México y de sus unidades económicas, también se encuentra un estudio detallado de los consumos en los sectores productivos, la generación distribuida y posibles acciones a tomar en cuenta por el gobierno. En este documento se presenta una serie de indicadores a través de un apartado con el mismo nombre, con la finalidad de tener una comprensión más profunda del contexto energético de la Ciudad de México.

The Ankara Metropolitan Municipality has undertaken comprehensive energy-related assessments as part of its Sustainable Energy and Climate Action Plan (SECAP, 2021) and its Local Climate Change Adaptation and Mitigation Action Plan (LCCAMAP). These assessments analyze energy access, security, sustainability, and affordability, fully aligned with the Global Covenant of Mayors for Climate and Energy (GCoM) Common Reporting Framework (CRF).

The assessments addressed the three key energy attributes of the GCoM Energy Access and Poverty Pillar (EAPP):

Sustainable Energy - Analysis of renewable energy potential, including municipal solar power projects, landfill biogas-to-energy plants, and energy efficiency improvements in public buildings and transport.

Secure Energy - Evaluation of resilience against climate-related risks such as heatwaves, water scarcity, and import dependency on fossil fuels, with diversification and local renewable sources identified as priorities.

Affordable Energy - Assessment of energy poverty, including the share of household income spent on energy, efficiency retrofit programs, subsidies for efficient appliances, and solar irrigation systems provided for rural communities.

The LCCAMAP Greenhouse Gas (GHG) Emission Inventory Report (2020), compiled using the City Inventory Reporting and Information System (CIRIS) tool, shows that stationary energy (residential, commercial, industrial) is the largest contributor to emissions, followed by transportation and waste. The total jurisdiction-wide energy consumption was approximately 32.5 million megawatt-hours (MWh), of which around 1.2 million MWh (about 3.5-4%) came from renewable sources.

Renewable energy sources included:

Solar Photovoltaic (PV): Rooftop PV installations on municipal facilities and rural irrigation systems.

Biogas-to-Energy: The Mamak Integrated Solid Waste Management Plant converts landfill gas into electricity.

Hydropower: Supplied through the national grid, complementing local renewable efforts.

Biomass: Small-scale agricultural biomass use, with future expansion potential.

Electricity mix: Ankara relies on the Turkish national grid, which is dominated by natural gas and coal, though the share of solar, wind, and hydro is increasing. ABB supplements this with green energy purchase agreements and local solar installations.

Thermal energy: Predominantly natural gas for heating in residential and commercial sectors. District heating, building insulation, and retrofits are targeted as priority measures to improve efficiency.

Key energy-related institutions and programs:

Ankara Water and Sewerage Administration (AWSA): Implements solar-powered pumping, water-saving campaigns, and distribution of efficiency devices.

Ankara Electricity and Gas Administration (AEGA): Expands metro systems, deploys electric buses, and promotes public transport incentives such as “Park & Ride.”

Rural Renewable Support Programs: Includes solar irrigation systems for farmers, indigenous seed support, and training for sustainable energy practices.

Waste-to-Energy: Landfill biogas capture and utilization through the Mamak facility.

Energy poverty measures: ABB has introduced programs to ensure that vulnerable households access affordable energy. These include efficiency retrofits, subsidies, distribution of conservation devices, and renewable energy support for rural communities.

Energy security considerations: The LCCAMAP Climate Risk and Vulnerability Assessment (CRVA) highlighted that Ankara's dependence on imported natural gas creates vulnerability to supply disruptions and price volatility. Scaling up renewables and improving efficiency are central to strengthening resilience.

Alignment with Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs):

SDG 7 - Affordable and Clean Energy

SDG 11 - Sustainable Cities and Communities

SDG 13 - Climate Action
References and URLs:
•	Sustainable Energy and Climate Action Plan (SECAP, 2021) - https://s.ankara.bel.tr/files/2025/08/15/f42313fc846b7ea1e79493e25be5e4d7.pdf
•	Ankara Green City Action Plan (GCAP, 2021) - https://www.ankara.bel.tr/files/2022/06/22/e6828f0c69930859c92414b0657fa2cd.pdf
Through these initiatives, Ankara Metropolitan Municipality demonstrates an integrated strategy combining technical measures (renewables, efficiency, electrification) with social programs (energy poverty alleviation, rural support, resilience building). This approach ensures compliance with GCoM EAPP while tailoring solutions to the local context of Ankara.

The City is continuously improving the accuracy and quality of the data it collects to calculate its inventory. At the time of reporting the City is in the process of a complete review of data sources and estimation methodologies as part of its State of Energy and Carbon 2025 publication. Funding for an extensive program of enhancements supported by an external technical specialist was obtained in 2023 and a contract awarded in November 2024 after an open tender process, the first for this exercise. Previous iterations have either been internal or grant funded.
 
The service provider has developed new accounting tools to address the many data challenges that occur at local level jurisdictions in developing countries. Methodologies have been revised to better integrate newer higher quality data sources such as the survey of larger scheduled emitters (SAGERS) by the Department of Forestry Fisheries and the Environment with older sources and insights from stakeholder engagement with the oil industry. Significantly, the service provider has increased the scope of the inventory to BASIC+ through estimating AFOLU and IPPU emissions, including the significant contribution of demand-side HFCs from air-conditioning units. In certain cases, assumptions, such as transmission loss factors have been reviewed, introducing significant changes. Additionally, the reporting year, 2023 saw very large step changes in the energy system, foremost amongst them extreme levels of power cuts imposed by the national system operator with some level of national load curtailment being imposed for 6335 hours and customers being disconnected on average for 792 hours during the year. As a result of this national supply crisis, the large peaking plant within the jurisdiction operated at a very high capacity factor. This combined with the accelerating recovery of the aviation industry after COVID and the resumption of full operations by the local refinery after a fire related closure, caused petroleum fuel energy use to increase within the jurisdiction even while electricity demand was severely impaired. 
 
While there are continuous improvements in the quality of data and estimation methodologies for internal operations, and for the sectors which the City has its own data such as solid waste, wastewater, and electricity (CCT electricity sales data). There continues to be inconsistencies in the data collected from external stakeholders (national entities in particular). Our dependence on these data sources for key sectors such as Transport, and a proportion of electricity consumption supplied by the national distribution subsidiary of state utility, Eskom remain ongoing challenges.

Regarding figures provided in this section : Total energy consumption includes all energy carriers and sources including electricity losses from both supply areas, SSEG on-site consumption, aviation and marine fuels and solar thermal energy from domestic solar water heaters. Total renewable energy includes total SSEG generation, solar thermal energy and renewable energy embedded in the grid energy mix. 
Theincrease in total energy consumption from last year is a result of the return to full operation of a petroleum refinery plant located in the jurisdiction, and the continued recovery of the aviation and marine navigation sectors after the impacts of the Covid 19 pandemic between 2020 and 2022. A 7.8% reduction in total energy consumption from renewable sources from 1 602 553 in 2022 is due to the decline in total electricity consumption which includes renewable electricity supply.

In addition, the data serves as an essential input for the City's GHG inventory and targets tracking. The report is available at the link below and the full data set is also on the City's Open Data Portal. column19: Campinas possui registrado no banco de dados da ANEEL um total de 9.455 (Comercio, residências, industrias e instituições públicas ) micro geradoras de sistema fotovoltaico instalado. A potência total consultada em 2023 era de 76.375 KW. Em seguida, estima-se a produção anual de energia elétrica em kWh (quilowatt-hora) usando dados típicos para a região de Campinas, SP. A produção anual média de um sistema solar fotovoltaico pode variar de 1.200 a 1.600 kWh/kWp, dependendo dos fatores mencionados acima (radiação solar, inclinação, orientação, etc.). Usando uma estimativa conservadora de 1.300 kWh/kWp, podemos calcular a energia gerada anualmente: Energia anual = 76.375 KW X 4,2 hora de luz útil do dia X 365 (dias do ano) = 117.084.300 kWh. Portanto, uma potência instalada de 76.375 kW de placas solares em Campinas, SP, poderia gerar aproximadamente 117.084.300 kWh de energia elétrica em um ano. É importante notar que esses cálculos são apenas estimativas e a produção real pode variar ao longo do ano, devido às variações climáticas e outros fatores. Considerando que os sistemas solares são injetados na rede e todos os usuários consomem essa energia renovável gerada no município, entendemos que é uma aproximação pertinente.

Realizamos uma avaliação do consumo de energia elétrica em Salvador com base nos dados públicos de consumo per capita de 2024 (média mensal em kWh por habitante - EPE) e na população do Censo 2022, de 2.417.678 pessoas. O consumo total estimado de eletricidade foi de aproximadamente 4.272.520,56 MWh/ano.

O painel público da ANEEL disponibiliza dados por município sobre a capacidade instalada, discriminados por tipo de tecnologia. Em Salvador, conforme a atualização mais recente, a capacidade instalada de geração distribuída totaliza 137.273,76 kW, sendo composta majoritariamente por sistemas fotovoltaicos solares, que representam mais de 99% do total.

Adicionalmente, avaliamos o potencial de geração de energia renovável com base nessa capacidade instalada. Utilizando um fator de capacidade conservador de 18% para a energia solar fotovoltaica, estimamos uma geração anual de aproximadamente 216.453,26 MWh, o que corresponde a cerca de 5,1% do consumo total de eletricidade do município.

The Energy balance assesses the stability and reliability of energy supply, focusing on local and external sources that contribute to energy security. The energy balance is prepared in accordance with the Eurostat methodology.

The data shows trends in energy consumption and dependency, indicating efforts to enhance secure energy through diversified energy sources, including local renewable generation and system resilience.

The assessment includes the analysis of renewable energy sources, which are critical to the city's efforts to achieve sustainability goals. 

In 2024, the total energy consumption from renewable energy sources was 1165861 MWh (15 %). The increase in the share of renewable energy is aimed at contributing to the overall reduction of greenhouse gas emissions and supporting long-term sustainability.

A major concern in the document is the affordability of energy for all residents, focusing on ensuring that energy prices are maintained at levels that do not disproportionately impact low-income households.

In 2024, a plan for the decarbonization of the district heating system by 2030 was prepared. This plan outlines the transition from coal and natural gas to renewable energy sources and the integration of renewable gases into the pipeline network. The document discusses the shift from fossil fuels to cheaper renewable sources taking in consideration as well energy poverty. Attached in Section 11.1.

column19: Of course, we are dealing with sustainable, safe and affordable energy. Germany's largest hard coal-fired power plant is operated on the Mannheim site, which makes an important contribution to security of energy supply. In the course of the energy transition, we want to replace fossil fuels with renewable energies as much as possible. This necessary transformation will change Mannheim's role from energy exporter for the region to energy importer. It is therefore all the more important for us to identify all renewable potentials in order to ensure a sustainable, secure and affordable energy supply in the coming years.One example of how we are doing this is the energy framework study, which examined these potentials and outlined a climate-neutral energy supply. At the time, the study had the target of climate neutrality in 2050, but in the context of our updated SECAP it was also recalculated to 2030.The Mannheim energy supplier \'MVV\' also supports the city's goal and is pursuing plans to supply climate-neutral district heating by 2030 and to be climate-positive from 2035. By the way, MVV is the first German and one of the first three energy companies worldwide whose targets have been verified as Net Zero compatible by the Science Based Targets Initiative (SBTi).

Medición y Reporte de Sostenibilidad General:
 Reportes de Sostenibilidad: EPEC elabora informes anuales desde 2020 adhiriéndose a los Estándares GRI (Global Reporting Initiative). Estos reportes evalúan el desempeño económico, ambiental y social de la empresa, alineando sus acciones con los 17 Objetivos de Desarrollo Sostenible (ODS) y los 10 Principios del Pacto Global de las Naciones Unidas.
 Planificación Estratégica y Control de Gestión: La Gerencia de Planificación Estratégica y Control de Gestión diseña y monitorea indicadores. Utilizan tableros de uso online para el seguimiento en tiempo real de la evolución acumulada, mensual y anual de los indicadores así como sus variaciones. En 2023 se implementaron 52 nuevos indicadores y 60 tableros para fortalecer este sistema.
Generación de Energía:
 Cuantificación de Energía Renovable: Se cuantifica la energía generada por sus Pequeños Aprovechamientos Hidráulicos (PAH). En el periodo reportado de 2023, los PAH generaron 2.367,56 MWh de energía renovable. 
El Proyecto Maipú de Generación Distribuida Comunitaria, basado en paneles solares, generó aproximadamente 1.407.600 kWh al año en 2023.
 Certificaciones de Calidad y Ambiente: Las centrales de generación más importantes de EPEC, como Bicentenario y Río Grande, han obtenido certificaciones trinorma (ISO 9001:2015 para Calidad, ISO 14001:2015 para Gestión Ambiental, e ISO 45001:2015 para Seguridad y Salud Ocupacional), demostrando excelencia en sus operaciones y cumplimiento de estándares internacionales. Otras centrales mantienen la certificación ISO 14001:2015.
Transmisión de Energía:
 Indicadores de Rendimiento de la Red: La red de transmisión se evalúa mediante métricas clave:
 *Tasa de Falla: Mide la frecuencia de averías, calculada como la cantidad de Salidas Forzadas de Líneas de Alta Tensión cada 100 km. En 2023, hubo un incremento del 7.8% debido a factores climáticos.
 * Energía No Suministrada (ENS): Refleja la cantidad de energía que no se entrega por interrupciones. En 2023, la ENS disminuyó un 39.7% en comparación con 2022, gracias al reemplazo de componentes.
 *Cantidad de Salidas Forzadas: Registra las desconexiones inesperadas de equipos. En 2023, se observó un aumento del 4% debido a incendios y tormentas.
 *Disponibilidad: Mide la proporción de tiempo que la red está operativa y disponible para transmitir energía.
Distribución de Energía y Calidad de Servicio:
 Indicadores de Calidad de Servicio: Para evaluar la calidad del servicio de distribución, se emplean los índices de interrupción FMIK (Frecuencia Media) y DMIK (Duración Media) por kVA nominal instalado, establecidos por el Ente Regulador de los Servicios Públicos (ERSeP). En 2023, los objetivos mejorados (FMIK = 4 y DMIK = 1,1) fueron cumplidos en ambos semestres.
 Telemedición y Sistemas Inteligentes: EPEC ha avanzado en la telemedición de subestaciones MT/BT en la ciudad de Córdoba, alcanzando el 56% telemedidas, lo que permite el monitoreo a distancia y la gestión en tiempo real de interrupciones.
 Tecnología de Medición Inteligente: Se están implementando nuevos medidores inteligentes para 200 mil usuarios, que permiten consultar el consumo casi en tiempo real, realizar cortes y reconexiones a distancia, y en el futuro, aplicar tarifas por bandas horarias. También se han implementado sistemas como el Meter Data Collector (MDC) y el Meter Data Management (MDM) para mejorar el control y la recolección de datos.
Gestión Ambiental y Huella de Carbono:
 Medición de Huella de Carbono: EPEC calcula anualmente su huella de carbono siguiendo la Norma IRAM-ISO 14.064-1 y el GHG Protocol. Se evalúan las emisiones directas (Alcance 1), indirectas por energía importada (Alcance 2) y otras indirectas (Alcance 3).
 Resultados de la Huella: En 2022, la huella total de las operaciones fue de 2.670.003 tCO2e. Se reportan las emisiones evitadas por centrales hidroeléctricas, que en 2022 fueron de 163.007 tnCO2e.
 Estrategias de Mitigación: EPEC evalúa el impacto de sus iniciativas de mitigación, como el aumento del uso de biocombustibles en su flota (evitando 25 tnCO2 en 2022), la digitalización de documentos, la generación solar fotovoltaica (evitando 11 tnCO2e) y el uso de vehículos eléctricos (evitando 2 tnCO2e en 2022).
Uso y Gestión de Recursos Específicos:
 Agua: Se monitorea la extracción de agua para sus centrales térmicas, registrando 2.916.260,50 metros cúbicos en 2023. Además, se utiliza el Indicador Internacional CIER 14 ('Uso específico de agua anual' en m3/MWh) para optimizar su consumo.
 Gas Natural: Se registra el consumo anual en metros cúbicos. En 2023, se observó un descenso significativo a 48.128,09 m3 desde 56.002,25 m3 en 2022.
Combustibles y Biocombustibles: Se evalúa el consumo de biocombustibles (Gasoil B20 y nafta E17), el cual creció un 396,53% en 2023, alcanzando 368.423,07 litros. Esto contribuyó a una disminución del 8,40% en el consumo de combustibles fosiles.

En términos de suministro, la electricidad de Saltillo y sus productos de
petróleo y gas son, en su mayor parte, proporcionados por la Comisión
Federal de Electricidad (CFE), la empresa estatal de electricidad de
México y Petróleos Mexicanos (PEMEX). Estas empresas han representado
la columna vertebral del sector energético de México. De hecho, la CFE
produce más de la mitad de la demanda eléctrica del país, posee más del
60 % de la capacidad de generación y, hasta hace poco, se mantuvo como
único proveedor minorista del país (IEA, 2017). Asimismo, PEMEX y sus
subsidiarias producen y abastecen a nivel nacional una fracción considerable
de la demanda total de petróleo de México, con una producción cercana
a 1,65 millones de barriles por día, en contraste con la demanda de México
de aproximadamente 2 millones de barriles por día.
La electricidad de Saltillo es suministrada por la red nacional de México,
que se basa principalmente en electricidad a partir de combustibles
fósiles, como se puede observar en la Gráfica 20, principalmente gas
natural (60 %), seguido por petróleo (10 %) y carbón (9 %). Las fuentes de
electricidad limpias y bajas en carbono representan el resto, con la energía
hidroeléctrica el 7 %, la eólica el 5 %, la nuclear el 3 % y la geotérmica y
solar 2 %. Como reflejo de la gran proporción de gas en la red, el factor de
emisión de CO2 de la red eléctrica asciende a 473 gramos de CO2 por KWh.

Every year, the municipality of Nijmegen draws up an energy monitoring report with data on the total energy consumption and production in the city (gas and electricity). The report provides insight into energy consumption from 2008 to 2023. The report can be viewed at DOCUMENT: NIEUW LINK TOEVOEGEN

Assesment that consider affordable energy: The municipality of Nijmegen has insight into the degree of energy poverty per district. We speak of energy poverty when a household has insufficient access to good energy supplies in the home. The Dutch Organization for Applied Scientific Research (TNO) conducted a broad national study into energy poverty in the Netherlands for the first time in 2021 (TNO, De energiearmoedekloof in Nederland, Een microdata-analyse van het niveau en 
de ongelijkheid van energiearmoede, 2024 TNO 2024 R11693 , 16 September 2025,
DOCUMENT https://publications.tno.nl/publication/34643138/yulKz7av/TNO-2024-R11693.pdf ). 

As a follow-up to TNO's research, the national Central Bureau of Statistics (CBS) has set up an annual Energy Poverty Monitoring on behalf of the Ministry of Economic Affairs and Climate. The table with energy poverty monitoring data at district level for all cities in the Netherlands can be found via the Energy Poverty Monitor 2020 website DOCUMENT https://www.cbs.nl/nl-nl/maatwerk/2023/04/monitor-energiearmoede-2020 under the heading 'downloads'. For Nijmegen, data is available from 44 neighborhoods for the years 2019 and 2020. In the monitoring report, CBS distinguishes five different indicators to determine the degree of energy poverty. Based on the LIHELEK indicator - Low income, high energy bill or low energetic quality - there are 5,748 households in Nijmegen with energy poverty for the year 2020, of which 848 are private renters, 4,443 social housing associations and 432 homeowners. As expected, the highest levels of energy poverty can be found in the social housing association's rental properties.Based on monitoring data from TNO and CBS, the municipality of Nijmegen has drawn up an approach to energy poverty in Nijmegen in 2021. DOCUMENT: https://nijmegen.bestuurlijkeinformatie.nl/Agenda/Document/6b5205a3-ad56-4e6a-ab42-5686b2b90075?documentId=357fc3c4-8aec-430f-ae1d-304b8ccc7618&agendaItemId=11a14876-e507-4b9a-9559-9268a35db80b# The actions are mentioned separately in the Mitigation Actions chapter (chapter 9).

The City Council concluded a Strategic Energy Advisor study with Jacobs which confirmed four key priority areas:
• Overall Land Supply - identify opportunities and constraints within Sunderland, evaluating land availability, determining viable energy solutions, to create a hierarchy of strategic energy sites and projects. The Council now has an interactive GIS based dashboard land assessment of technically viable sites for renewable energy generation, this is helping to inform policy decisions on future land use.
• Council Property - the Energy Services team within the Council identified opportunities and constraints within Sunderland City Council's major operational properties, evaluating fabric improvements, HVAC improvements, as well as generation and storage opportunities shortlisting viable solutions. Capital investment was then secured from the Council Capital programme (£3.6million to support 13 buildings), alongside PSDS3c (£2.42million for 4 buildings) and £1.07 million from PSDS4 to decarbonise the Sunderland Crematorium.
• Port of Sunderland - Energy Hub; examining larger scale opportunities in wind offshore and onshore, PV, battery storage, Green Hydrogen over the short, medium, and long term and identifying any constraints. 'Think Piece' on the Port as a developing Energy Hub for the city within its real estate is needed to test the land assets necessary as part of a future masterplan. As a result discussions are ongoing with potential renewable energy developers.
• Development Standards; The council continues to conduct a review of the current range of buildings and designs /targets for each sector/type of construction, bring compare the benchmark of Sunderland's approach including what impact this might have on cost /viability for the City's geographic area and market. Test compliance of the benchmarks chosen for the existing programme with new and emerging building standards in each sector and to suggest any improvement areas set against the city carbon targets. Assess whether there can be a standardised approach to both private development /developers and public build programmes in terms of standards on fabric /build/energy and decarbonisation technologies in terms of embodied carbon/ carbon in operation and overall energy efficiency. Test “future proofing” fabric/ technology flexibility /standards and targets set with those achieved elsewhere with emerging standards with relevant examples and case studies.

column19: Pobreza energética é a incapacidade de manter a habitação com um nível adequado de serviços energéticos essenciais, devido a uma combinação de baixos rendimentos, baixo desempenho energético da habitação e custo com energia. Este projeto de Gestão da Pobreza Energética no Setor Doméstico Social, pretende identificar, caraterizar, atuar e monitorizar os agregados que habitam em 256 habitações de um município da CIM do Ave (Guimarães).O principal indicador de pobreza energética é quando um agregado familiar gasta 10% ou mais do seu rendimento monetário em despesas energéticas e se situa abaixo da Linha de Pobreza definida como 60% do rendimento mediano por adulto equivalente. O projeto que se apresenta, com a elaboração de um Plano de Ação, pretende criar uma ferramenta que, mediante o diagnóstico, identifique antecipadamente situações de Pobreza Energética, e oriente os diversos atores para as soluções a adotar. A 1.ª fase do trabalho identifica as ações a implementar, identificando os respetivos promotores e instrumentos de financiamento. Ou seja, criar as condições para que possa ser elaborado um Plano de Ação municipal no combate à pobreza energética no Setor Doméstico Social. A 2.ª fase será a implementação do Plano de Ação proposto para a obtenção das metas definidas.\nA produção e consumo de energia renovável está presente em Guimarães desde 1912. Cinco centrais mini-hídricas produzem aproximadamente 15 GWh/ano. Atualmente os resíduos verdes produzidos das ações de manutenção de espaços verdes e jardins produzem 120 toneladas de biomassa (0.5 GWh/ano). Guimarães é o concelho a nível nacional com maior potência fotovoltaica instalada (53,113 MWh), com uma produção estimada de 80 GWh/ano. Combinadas, estas fontes de energia cobrem o equivalente a 47% da energia elétrica consumida pelo setor doméstico.

column19: As Alterações Climáticas são uma realidade com impactos ambientais, sociais e económicos. Neste contexto, reduzir significativamente as emissões de Gases com Efeito de Estufa (GEE) através da construção de uma economia de baixo carbono é uma prioridade. Uma aposta em inovação e no investimento em tecnologias verdes permitirá alcançar uma sociedade de baixas emissões e, simultaneamente, impulsionar a economia, criar empregos e reforçar a competitividade do município. O Município de Águeda tem conduzido projetos inovadores na temática da sustentabilidade ambiental e climática, a par de um desenvolvimento evidente ao nível social e económico. No dia 12 de novembro de 2008, o Município de Águeda aderiu ao Pacto de Autarcas, assumindo o compromisso de reduzir as emissões de CO2 no seu território em 33% até 2020. Atualmente, o Município pretende atualizar este compromisso, adotando uma abordagem integrada à atenuação e adaptação às Alterações Climáticas e assumindo o objetivo de ultrapassar a meta de redução de 55% de emissões de CO2 até 2030, a redução da pobreza energética e a criação de uma visão a longo prazo para alcançar a neutralidade climática até 2050, através de uma transição justa. De modo a alcançar as metas propostas o município desenvolveu o presente Plano de Ação para a Energia Sustentável e o Clima (PAESC), o qual define diversas medidas de mitigação e adaptação às Alterações Climáticas. O objetivo de redução de emissões de CO2 no território concelhio deverá ser alcançado através de um aumento da eficiência energética e de uma produção e utilização mais limpa da energia, tal como formulado no Pacote de Medidas da União Europeia sobre o Clima e as Energias Renováveis. Na vertente de adaptação às Alterações Climáticas são propostas ações com o objetivo de adaptação ou mitigação dos efeitos destas alterações. Estas ações vão desde ações de educação e sensibilização ambiental, adoção de sistemas de monitorização, avaliação e vigilância, reforço de infraestruturas verdes e gestão sustentável da floresta, ordenamento e gestão dos recursos fluviais e espécies florestais e agrícolas, controlo de pragas e doenças, entre outros. De modo a cumprir este compromisso, o município compromete-se a definir diversas medidas de sustentabilidade energética que integram o Plano de Ação para a Energia Sustentável e o Clima (PAESC). O PAESC identifica eventuais situações com potencial de melhoria, tendo como base a avaliação contínua de indicadores. Estes indicadores são definidos de acordo com as recomendações do Pacto de Autarcas e do Joint Research Center. Este plano apresenta um inventário de referência de emissões, no qual se pretende quantificar os consumos energéticos e as emissões de CO2 inerentes à atividade desenvolvida no município (tendo como referência o ano de 2002) e uma Avaliação dos Riscos e da Vulnerabilidades às Alterações Climáticas.

O concelho de Braga, um dos mais importantes do norte de Portugal, possui um consumo total de energia de 3.654.595 MWh, dos quais 730.919 MWh (20%) provêm de fontes renováveis. Esta distribuição energética reflete o compromisso crescente do município com a transição para uma matriz energética mais sustentável, embora ainda existam desafios significativos.

A gestão energética em Braga é organizada em três níveis: decisão, gestão e implementação. As decisões políticas são tomadas pela Câmara Municipal, em articulação com a Comunidade Intermunicipal do Cávado. A implementação é realizada pela empresa E-REDES, contratada para executar o Plano Anual de Obras, enquanto a ADENE, entidade pública responsável por auditorias energéticas, assegura que os edifícios cumprem os padrões de eficiência energética. As associações empresariais, como a Associação Comercial de Braga e a Associação Empresarial do Minho, desempenham um papel crucial na promoção de práticas de eficiência energética no setor comercial e industrial.

A mobilidade é um fator importante no consumo energético de Braga. Apesar de metade da população ainda usar veículos privados, houve um aumento significativo no uso de transporte público, com 12,7 milhões de passageiros em 2023, o que indica uma mudança para modos de transporte mais sustentáveis. O município tem trabalhado na expansão da infraestrutura de ciclovias e na melhoria da rede de transportes públicos, incentivando uma mobilidade mais sustentável.

No setor residencial, que é um dos maiores consumidores de energia, Braga tem promovido a modernização de edifícios e a instalação de sistemas de energia solar, mas a adesão ainda é limitada. As iniciativas de eficiência energética visam reduzir o consumo, especialmente durante o inverno, quando o uso de aquecimento elétrico aumenta.

O setor comercial e industrial também consome uma parte significativa da energia de Braga. Projetos de modernização de iluminação, automação e adoção de energias renováveis estão em curso, especialmente em grandes empresas. No entanto, as pequenas e médias empresas (PMEs) enfrentam desafios maiores para implementar essas tecnologias, sendo necessárias iniciativas de apoio financeiro e capacitação.

A infraestrutura energética de Braga tem sido modernizada, com investimentos em redes inteligentes e a expansão da rede de carregamento de veículos elétricos. No entanto, a integração de energias renováveis na rede elétrica e a adaptação das tecnologias existentes ainda são desafios significativos.

A transição energética em Braga enfrenta obstáculos, como o equilíbrio entre crescimento económico e sustentabilidade ambiental, e a necessidade de maior conscientização pública. Contudo, também oferece oportunidades, como a criação de empregos no setor de energia verde e o posicionamento da cidade como um modelo de sustentabilidade.

Em resumo, Braga demonstra um compromisso sólido com a eficiência energética e a transição para fontes renováveis, mas precisa continuar a investir em tecnologias verdes e educação ambiental para superar os desafios e garantir um futuro mais sustentável e resiliente.

Çanakkale Municipality has undertaken various energy-related initiatives to enhance sustainability and reduce carbon emissions. One of the most significant projects is the solar power plant established at the Wastewater Treatment Facility, covering an area of 14,550 m². This solar farm has a total capacity of 992.8 kW and consists of 3,828 locally manufactured 280-watt panels.

The Municipality has successfully addressed the energy needs of its environmentally friendly investments through equally environmentally friendly energy solutions. The wastewater treatment process is powered by solar energy, and sludge drying operations at the solar drying facility are also carried out using solar power. Thanks to this circular system, our city has earned Blue Flag beaches, an important eco-label indicating high environmental quality. Although these initiatives may appear to be separate investments, when viewed from a broader perspective, they are clearly integrated components of a large-scale environmental project.

From 2019 to the present, a total of 8,250 MWh of electricity has been produced, preventing 4,158 tons of carbon emissions.

Following a national project competition, construction of the Municipal Service Building began in 2015 and was completed in 2023. The building was designed and constructed in accordance with the criteria for the GOLD LEED “Green Building Certification.” The facility has a total indoor area of 27,083 m², including:

A parking lot for 172 vehicles,

A wedding hall with a capacity of 370 people,

A municipal council hall,

A multi-purpose hall with a capacity of 780 people,

700 m² of foyer space, and

A 380 m² exhibition area forming the Cultural Center.

A rooftop solar power system consisting of 914 panels with a total capacity of 301.62 kW has been installed on the Service Building and Cultural Center. Since its commissioning in 2023, this system has generated 1,120 MWh of electricity and prevented 534 tons of carbon emissions.

Additionally, a solar power system with 864 panels and a capacity of 354.24 kW has been installed on the buildings within the Municipality's Technical Services Campus. Since 2023, this system has generated 844.36 MWh of electricity and prevented 401 tons of carbon emissions.

Furthermore, national regulations requiring new buildings to comply with nearly zero-energy building (nZEB) standards are enforced in Çanakkale. Under these regulations, the mandatory share of renewable energy usage in new buildings initially set at 5% has increased to 10% as of 2025. These measures contribute significantly to reducing the municipality's overall energy consumption and carbon footprint.

Beşiktaş Municipality has undertaken a comprehensive assessment of energy consumption across the entire district, covering both residential, commercial, and public buildings as well as the transportation sector. This detailed evaluation is aligned with the Sustainable Energy and Climate Action Plan (SECAP), which outlines the district's commitment to reducing carbon emissions and transitioning toward a more sustainable energy system. The data collected from these assessments provide insights into the total energy consumption, broken down by fuel type, sector, and usage, allowing for an accurate understanding of how energy is being consumed and where improvements can be made.

In terms of emissions reporting, Beşiktaş Municipality has measured energy consumption in various sectors such as stationary energy use (including heating and cooling systems), transportation, and industrial processes. The energy data collected are translated into CO2 equivalent emissions, helping the municipality to better understand its carbon footprint and target key areas for reduction. This data is essential for tracking progress toward the municipality's long-term goals of reducing greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions, improving energy efficiency, and increasing the share of renewable energy sources in the overall energy mix.

One of the core objectives of Beşiktaş's energy-related assessments is to ensure alignment with the broader goals of energy sustainability, energy security, and affordability. The assessments consider not only how energy is consumed but also how it can be sourced more sustainably. By focusing on renewable energy technologies such as solar and wind, the municipality is working toward reducing its reliance on fossil fuels and increasing the local generation of clean energy. The SECAP provides a roadmap for achieving these goals, including specific targets for reducing energy consumption and carbon emissions by 2030.

The energy assessments also take into account the affordability of energy, ensuring that the transition to renewable energy sources and energy efficiency improvements does not disproportionately impact vulnerable populations. Beşiktaş Municipality is committed to ensuring that clean energy is accessible to all residents, while also maintaining a reliable and secure energy supply.

These assessments and the data derived from them are publicly available and have been shared with stakeholders to promote transparency and public engagement in the municipality's efforts to combat climate change. By making this information accessible, Beşiktaş Municipality encourages collaboration with local residents, businesses, and government entities to collectively work toward achieving the goals set out in the Sustainable Energy and Climate Action Plan.

For further information and detailed reports on Beşiktaş Municipality's energy consumption assessments, please refer to the Sustainable Energy and Climate Action Plan (SECAP) which outlines the district's ongoing and planned projects to reduce emissions and improve energy efficiency. The SECAP document is available on the official Beşiktaş Municipality website.

Web link to further information: https://cevre.besiktas.bel.tr/Uploads/cevre.besiktas.bel.tr/Dokuman/besiktas_secap_rapor.pdf

Energy Assessment
Kisumu undertook a Baseline Emissions Inventory (BEI) and Access to Energy Assessment (AEA) under the Covenant of Mayors in Sub‑Saharan Africa (CoM SSA) initiative. These studies gathered primary data from the seven sub‑counties, public institutions, households and SMEs.The BEI considered sectors like stationary energy (buildings), transport, waste, agriculture, forestry, industrial processes. It looked at greenhouse gases CO₂, CH₄, N₂O, etc.Energy system modelling was also done as part of the “100% Renewables” (100%RE) roadmap project, to develop transition pathways for electricity, transport, and cooking sectors.

Energy Consumption Patterns
Electricity access: roughly 60% of households have grid electricity. Among SMEs, about 86% are grid‑connected; somewhat over 10% of SMEs use solar solutions. All public institutions have electricity access. Cooking energy: dominant fuels are charcoal and firewood; many households still depend heavily on these traditional biomass sources for cooking. In informal settlements, non‑clean energy options dominate for both cooking and lighting. Socioeconomic factors (household size, education, gender of head, etc.) influence energy‑choices

https://www.comunaenergetica.cl/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/Informe-Estrategia-Energetica-local-Punta-Arenas.pdf

La Elaboración de la Estrategia Energética Local (EEL) de Punta Arenas fue un proceso participativo que involucró a la comunidad para planificar el desarrollo energético de la comuna. Se desarrollaron diagnósticos de consumo energético y estudios de vulnerabilidad, considerando tanto el sector residencial como comercial e industrial, lo que permitió levantar información clave sobre la gestión energética del territorio.

Actualmente, la matriz energética regional depende mayoritariamente del gas natural (64,8% del consumo final), seguido de derivados del petróleo, electricidad y biomasa. La generación eléctrica proviene del Sistema Eléctrico de Magallanes (SEM), con capacidad instalada neta de 104,41 MW, principalmente a partir de gas natural. La comuna también utiliza combustibles térmicos como kerosene, GLP, leña y gas natural, siendo este último favorecido por la producción local y subsidios de ENAP.

El diagnóstico identificó oportunidades de energías renovables (eólica, dendroenergía, solar, hidráulica, undimotriz, biogás y bioenergía), destacando la eólica con un potencial de 1.646 GWh/año y la dendroenergía con 615 GWh/año. Asimismo, se evaluaron medidas de eficiencia energética, como aislamiento térmico de viviendas y recambio a iluminación LED, que podrían reducir hasta un 40% el consumo térmico residencial y un 51% el consumo eléctrico por iluminación.

En cuanto a emisiones de CO₂, la comuna produce 280.000 ton CO₂ eq., equivalente a 2,1 ton per cápita, siendo el consumo térmico el principal aporte. El consumo energético total de 2019 fue de 6.473 GWh, proyectándose 6.657 GWh para 2030.

El proceso participativo permitió generar una visión energética comunal basada en las características territoriales y sectoriales, consolidando un Plan de Acción alineado con las seis categorías del Sello Comuna Energética. La implementación de la EEL se seguirá evaluando anualmente, con revisión de proyectos a corto, mediano y largo plazo hasta 2033, y una actualización del instrumento cada dos años para garantizar eficacia y eficiencia en el avance del plan.

column19:
The Catbalogan City Electric Supply Data 2024 provides a detailed picture of the city's electrification progress, energy consumption, and remaining challenges in ensuring universal access to clean and reliable electricity.

At the city-wide level, electrification coverage has reached 93% in rural areas, with 12,935 households connected to the grid and 941 still unserved. Urban areas, by comparison, show near-universal coverage, with reported figures exceeding 100% in some barangays. These anomalies likely reflect mismatches between population projections and actual household connections, but the data clearly illustrates that electricity access in the urban core is effectively universal. The remaining gap lies in remote rural and coastal barangays, where last-mile electrification is more difficult and costly to achieve.

Electricity consumption patterns also reveal steady growth across all user types, reflecting Catbalogan's increasing urbanization and economic activity. Residential households remain the dominant consumers, with more than 21,000 connections consuming 2.36 million kWh per month in 2024, up from 2.02 million in 2022. Commercial users also recorded rising demand, consuming 1.17 million kWh per month, while industrial users, though small in number (10 connections), continue to consume disproportionately high volumes of energy, averaging 349,248 kWh per month. Public buildings and street lighting also account for consistent, though smaller, shares of total demand. These trends highlight the dual role of energy supply: both as a driver of household welfare and as a critical enabler of commerce and industry.

At the barangay level, almost all communities are now energized either through direct grid connection or off-grid solutions such as diesel generators and solar home systems. High-performing barangays include Cabugawan, Lobo, Palanyogon, Muñoz, Pupua, San Pablo, and Socorro, each of which report coverage rates between 97% and 100%. Similarly, off-grid barangays such as Bagongon (99%), Buluan (96%), and Cagutsan (92%) are nearing universal household electrification. However, significant service gaps remain in barangays such as Manguehay (36%), Basiao (42%), Cawayan (51%), Libas (54%), and Poblacion 13 (13%), where large portions of households remain without electricity.

These disparities underline the last-mile challenge in Catbalogan's energy transition. While most urban residents enjoy reliable electricity, rural households — particularly in geographically isolated and disadvantaged areas — remain underserved. Some barangays also report coverage above 100% (such as Canlapwas at 117% and Poblacion 5 at 527%), which may indicate unrecorded household adjustments, data entry inconsistencies, or population estimates that no longer match current realities.

Overall, the 2024 data demonstrates substantial progress toward near-universal barangay electrification, but also emphasizes the need for targeted interventions in low-coverage barangays to achieve 100% household electrification. Coupled with rising demand in both residential and productive sectors, Catbalogan City must ensure that its energy strategy is not only about expanding access but also about improving affordability, reliability, and sustainability.

Listrik: ± 730.660 MWh/tahun (730,66 GWh), dengan dominasi rumah tangga (70%), lalu komersial/jasa (22%), industri kecil (5%), dan pemerintahan (3%).

BBM transportasi: menjadi kontributor energi terbesar setelah listrik, dengan pemakaian bensin, solar, dan pertalite untuk kendaraan bermotor.

LPG: dipakai luas di rumah tangga dan usaha kecil, menyumbang emisi CO₂ dan CH₄.

Renewable Energy Contribution
PLTS/solar cell: baru sekitar 1.200-1.500 MWh/tahun (<0,2% dari total konsumsi listrik).
Energi terbarukan lain (mikrohidro, biomassa) masih terbatas, belum terintegrasi signifikan dalam bauran energi kota.

Emission Assessment
Sektor energi menyumbang >60% emisi GRK Kota Manado, terutama dari transportasi berbasis BBM dan listrik berbasis fosil.
Intensitas emisi listrik dihitung menggunakan faktor emisi grid Sulawesi, sehingga setiap MWh konsumsi listrik dapat diturunkan jejak karbonnya jika bauran energi lebih hijau.

Konsumsi energi tumbuh ±6-7% per tahun (RPJMD).

Policy & Strategy
RPJMD mengarahkan pada efisiensi energi rumah tangga dan perkantoran, pengembangan transportasi rendah emisi, serta perluasan PLTS atap.

Kajian Nilai Ekonomi Karbon menekankan bahwa dekarbonisasi energi adalah kunci untuk mencapai target penurunan emisi, dengan mendorong investasi pada renewable energy dan green building.

The Utilities Department has been pursuing technical assistance and grant opportunities to conduct energy audits and renewable energy studies at the water treatment plants and the entire system. Additionally, effective February 1, 2025, the City of Boynton Beach has partnered with FP&L to participate n the FPL SolarTogether Program (Resolution No. R25-012). The City will offset 2.6 MW of electricity usage annually from demand accounts, with a payback period of approximately 7 years. \n\nThe Climate Action Plan has made considerations for sustainable energy throughout the city. The city has established a goal to become the leader in energy efficiency and clean energy that comes from the sun, wind, or other renewable technologies. The City received a 2010 Energy Efficiency Conservation Block Grant from the U.S. Department of Energy to complete the CAP as well as demonstration projects including five electric vehicle charging stations in City lots, solar panels and water heaters at Fire Station No. 5, and an energy-efficient lighting retrofit ofthe Ezell Hester Jr. Community Center. Adoption of the CAP (Resolution No. R10-150) was soon followed by the establishment of a voluntary Green Building Program (Ordinance No. 11-014). The City's Green Building Program received the 2011 Gala Verde Award for Green Outstanding Government by the U.S. Green Building Council's South Florida Chapter, and the CAP was awarded the 2012 Award for Program Excellence from the Florida City and County Management Association (FCCMA). The City released a revised CAP in 2015 (adopted via Resolution No. R15-166), which integrated recommendations of the 2012 RCAP and tracked the status of progress since 2010. The 2015 CAP highlighted recent accomplishments, such as updating the Comprehensive Plan Coastal Element to consider sea level rise and other flood risks as mandated by the 2015 Peril of Flood statute (S.B. 1094); adopting a Greenways, Blueways, and Trails Master Plan (Resolution No. R15-143); and establishing a Property Assessed Clean Energy (PACE) financing program (Ordinance No. 16-017).

O Município da Covilhã realizou diversas avaliações energéticas no âmbito do Plano de Ação para a Energia Sustentável e Clima (PAESC), aprovado em 2022, e do respetivo 1.º Relatório de Monitorização, publicado em 2025. Estes documentos incluem uma análise detalhada do consumo de energia final por setor (residencial, terciário, transportes, agricultura e edifícios municipais), bem como uma estimativa do consumo proveniente de fontes de energia renovável. Foram ainda incluídas avaliações da eficiência energética dos edifícios escolares e municipais, com propostas de melhoria, e a monitorização da evolução das emissões de CO₂ entre 2008 e 2023. No que diz respeito à pobreza energética, esta foi estimada com base na percentagem de residências dentro da jurisdição que enfrentam esta condição.

As avaliações energéticas permitiram analisar a composição por combustível nos setores residencial, terciário e agrícola, incluindo eletricidade, biomassa e derivados do petróleo. Foram também avaliados o consumo de energia térmica (aquecimento e refrigeração), a capacidade instalada de produção renovável e as medidas implementadas para promover a eficiência energética, como a substituição de luminárias por tecnologia LED, a reabilitação energética de edifícios e o reforço da mobilidade elétrica e sustentável.

Estas avaliações seguem as recomendações do Pacto de Autarcas e do Joint Research Centre (JRC) da União Europeia e estão alinhadas com os requisitos do Pilar de Acesso à Energia e Pobreza Energética (EAPP) do Global Covenant of Mayors for Climate and Energy (GCoM). 

Os documentos podem ser consultados através dos seguintes links: https://plantasonline.cm-covilha.pt/geoportal

Methodology for Estimating Renewable Energy Consumption by Sector (Borough-Level)

1. Electricity Sector
Data Source:
• Renewable electricity by local authority dataset (2014-2023) - Department for Business, Energy & Industrial Strategy (BEIS)
• LEGGI 2022 - Borough electricity consumption (Domestic + Industrial) in kWh
• DUKES 2023 - National grid renewable electricity proportion for 2022: 41.8%
Calculation:
Renewable electricity consumption = total borough fossil fuel electricity consumption x (renewable electricity proportion / 1000). 

2. Transport Sector
Data Source:
• LEGGI 2022 - Borough transport consumption (Railway diesel + Road transport fossil fuels) in kWh
• LEGGI 2022 - Bioenergy (7,559,640 kWh) + Waste (382,236,870 kWh) = 389,796,511 kWh
• DUKES 2023 - Transport fuels renewable proportion: 5.3%
Calculation:
Renewable transport consumption = total borough fossil fuel transport consumption x ( transport fuels renewable proportion / 1000).
 
3. Heat Sector
Data Source:
• LEGGI 2022 - Borough heat consumption (Domestic + Industrial Gas/Coal/Oil) in kWh
• DUKES 2023 - Heat fuels renewable proportion: 8.4%
• Calculation:
Renewable heat sector consumption = total borough fossil fuel heat consumption x (heat fuels renewable proportion / 1000). 

4. Bioenergy Sector
Data source:
• LEGGI 2022 - Borough heat consumption (Domestic bioenergy and waste) in kWh
• Calculation:
Bioenergy consumption = Domestic bioenergy and waste in kWh / 1000

5. Total electricity consumption
Data source:
• LEGGI 2022 - Borough kWh - Domestic Elec and Industrial electricity.
• Calculation:
Total electricity consumption = domestic elec + industrial electricity consumption
6. Local renewable electricity production
Data source:
https://www.gov.uk/government/statistics/regional-renewable-statistics

As emissões do setor de Energia Estacionária são oriundas da queima de combustíveis em
atividades associadas à produção de energia e ao uso final desta energia em fontes fixas. A
evolução das emissões brutas do setor de Energia Estacionária no município de Itabirito no
período de 2010 a 2019 está ilustrada no Gráfico 9, desagregada nos subsetores Industrial e
Residencial. Ressalta-se que as contribuições do subsetor Comercial foram muito pontuais,
registradas apenas em 2013 (0,62 mil tCO2e), 2014 (0,67 mil tCO2e), 2018 (0,26 mil tCO2e) e
2019 (0,24 mil tCO2e), e por este motivo não estão sendo demonstradas neste gráfico.
A evolução das emissões parece estar relacionada, majoritariamente, com o comportamento
das emissões relativas ao subsetor Industrial. Estas emissões apresentaram um crescimento
de 101% em relação ao ano de 2010, quando foi observada sua menor contribuição (16,69 mil
tCO2e), e o ano de 2018, quando foi observada sua maior contribuição (33,52 mil tCO2e). Ao
final desta série histórica (2019) foi observada a emissão de 29,72 mil tCO2e, o que representa
um crescimento de 78% no período analisado.
Por se tratar de um município que apresenta uma economia fortemente vinculada à atividade
minerária, é possível inferir que as emissões relativas ao subsetor Industrial em Itabirito sejam
oriundas, principalmente, de atividades relacionadas à mineração.
Já a contribuição do subsetor Residencial apresentou um crescimento de 59% em relação ao
ano de 2010, quando foi observada o menor quantitativo de emissão (4,86 mil tCO2e), e o ano
de 2018, quando foi observada o maior quantitativo (7,73 mil tCO2e). Ao final desta série
histórica (2019), com a emissão de 5,74 mil tCO2e, observa-se um crescimento de 18% no
período analisado.

Other Energy Sources: Developing other types such as hydropower (small), waste-to-energy, geothermal power, biogas power, and biomass power.

Hue is a city with a diverse energy profile that reflects both traditional fuel use and a growing shift toward renewable sources. In 2024, the province's total energy consumption was estimated at 6.57 million MWh, of which approximately 55% (3.61 million MWh) was derived from renewable energy sources. This high share highlights Vietnam's national transition toward greener energy and Hue's active participation in that process.
Electricity consumption remains a major component of the province's energy demand. In 2024, households, industries, and commercial services consumed more than two million MWh of electricity. Much of this electricity is supplied through the national grid, which integrates significant amounts of hydropower from local plants such as Huong Dien, Binh Dien, and A Luoi, as well as contributions from solar farms and a municipal waste-to-energy facility.
In addition to electricity, fossil fuels continue to play an important role. Diesel oil, gasoline, and coal are widely used in transportation, construction, and small industries. However, biomass and traditional fuels such as firewood are declining in importance as modern energy access expands.
Looking forward, Hue City aims to balance economic growth with sustainability. The province's reliance on hydropower and solar energy positions it as a leader in renewable integration in central Vietnam. Yet, challenges remain in improving efficiency, reducing dependency on imported fuels, and ensuring a reliable supply during seasonal variations. With the national target of carbon neutrality by mid-century, Hue's energy transition will be critical to both local development and Vietnam's broader climate commitments.

The “Electric Consumption Tally File” provides a detailed record of electricity use across government-owned facilities and services in the City of Carmona from 2018 to 2024. Organized into multiple sheets, the dataset allows the local government to track both annual and monthly electricity consumption, linking each facility or service to specific service IDs for accuracy. It covers key sites such as the City Hall compound, the public market, streetlights, community centers, and other government-operated buildings.

The file begins with a pivot summary of total kWh consumption per area, offering a quick view of yearly trends and cumulative totals. This makes it easier to identify whether overall energy use is rising or falling over time. Following this, the TOTAL sheet consolidates monthly data for all accounts, presenting not only consumption but also yearly totals and averages, which are useful for monitoring efficiency.

Each subsequent sheet, arranged by year from 2018 through 2024, provides granular monthly data for each electric meter. This structure enables year-on-year comparisons and supports the identification of high-consuming facilities that may benefit from energy-saving interventions. For example, the City Hall compound and the public market consistently appear as major consumers, reflecting their role as hubs of administrative and commercial activity. Streetlights, while individually lower in consumption, collectively represent a significant share of public service energy demand.

The Building-Service ID sheet serves as a reference table that ensures consistency in linking accounts to their respective facilities. This prevents duplication and provides clarity when interpreting large volumes of data across multiple years.

Overall, the dataset is more than just a tally of numbers—it is a tool for energy management and climate action planning. By analyzing the information, Carmona's LGU can better understand which facilities drive utility costs, identify opportunities for conservation, and integrate energy efficiency measures into both budget and climate resilience planning. The continuous documentation from 2018 to 2024 demonstrates not only accountability in resource use but also the potential to guide future decisions toward a low-carbon, cost-efficient municipal operation.

Here is a summary of the latest information (as of early and mid-2025) regarding Ca Mau province's energy sector:
1. Current Electricity Production and Capacity
In 2024, the province's electricity production reached 2,041 million kWh, marking a 25.76% increase since 2020 with an average annual growth rate of 5.83%. Commercial electricity output reached 1,932 million kWh, up 27.99%. The grid's peak capacity hit 339.7 MW. The electricity grid operates stably according to the N-1 criterion. The province has four fuel depots with a capacity of 5,600 m³ and 357 retail stores, meeting an annual consumption demand of over 200,000 m³.
2. Renewable Energy (Wind, Solar, Biomass, etc.)
•	Wind Power: As of mid-2025, the province has 14 wind power plants in operation with a total capacity of 694.2 MW. Additionally, 34 wind power projects (onshore, nearshore, and offshore) with a total capacity of 2,309 MW are being implemented under Power Master Plan VIII, with an expected completion before 2030.
•	Rooftop Solar: There are 2,827 installed rooftop solar systems with a total capacity of nearly 295.5 MWp. The province also plans for an additional 117 MW for self-produced, self-consumed solar power.
•	Further Renewable Potential: The province has significant potential for developing wind and solar power, as well as new energy sources like hydrogen (with a total potential production of green hydrogen of approximately 86,248 tonnes/year) in districts like Dam Doi and Ngoc Hien.
3. Energy Export Plans and Targets
According to Decision 48/QD-TTg (2023), the province is developing a plan to export renewable energy with the following goals:
•	2,000 MW by 2031
•	3,000 MW by 2035
•	5,000 MW by 2040
The province aims to become the 'southern energy development hub,' with a total established capacity of about 4,000 MW. The goal is to reach 1,000 MW of renewable energy by 2030, with an additional 5,000 MW by 2045. The province is also establishing investment mechanisms for green hydrogen production projects from renewable energy and electricity export systems, though some regulatory hurdles remain.
4. Oil, Gas, and LNG
The Ca Mau Gas-Power-Fertilizer Complex: As of February 2025, it has supplied 28.81 billion m³ of gas, generated 116.49 billion kWh of electricity, produced 11.18 million tonnes of fertilizer, achieved a revenue of approximately 336.42 trillion VND, and contributed over 21 trillion VND to the state budget. The province plans to build offshore gas pipelines from the Nam Du-U Minh fields to PM3-Ca Mau (capacity of about 0.5-2.4 billion m³/year), as well as an LNG FSRU system to import 1-3 million tonnes of gas per year, expected to be operational between 2026 and 2030.
5. Energy Conservation and Efficiency
2024 Energy Conservation and Efficiency Plan: The province has set a target to conserve 2-4% of its total energy consumption, reduce power loss to below 3.5%, and implement energy management systems for 100% of its key energy-intensive facilities. The plan also emphasizes promoting communication and implementing solutions in both businesses and public life.

column19:
The energy landscape in Phu Yen province, Vietnam, is defined by its strategic focus on Renewable Energy (RE) development, particularly solar power, which leverages the province's favorable natural resources. Energy assessments primarily reflect the transition toward cleaner sources while also highlighting challenges in efficiency and infrastructure management.
1. Energy Consumption Profile
•	Reliable Supply: Phu Yen has largely overcome localized power shortages, successfully meeting the electricity demands for both residential use and industrial production.
•	Household Consumption: A study in Tuy Hoa City indicated that household energy consumption is mainly met by electricity and Liquid Petroleum Gas (LPG). Electricity accounts for about 74.4% of the energy consumed by a typical household, with the largest end-use being cooling (31.9%).
•	Industry and Economic Growth: The province is focusing on attracting investments and ensuring that the power supply supports its economic growth (GRDP) across all sectors, including the industrial and construction sectors.
2. Renewable Energy Development and Assessment
Phu Yen is recognized as a key area for solar and wind energy development in Vietnam's South-Central Coast region.
•	Solar Power Dominance: The province possesses high solar radiation potential (ranging from 4.9 to 5.7 kWh/m²/day), which has led to a rapid surge in solar projects. The operational solar capacity is significant, including one of the largest single operating solar power plants in Vietnam (a 257 MW project).
•	Hydropower Contribution: Large-scale hydropower plants, such as Song Ba Ha, are also major contributors to the province's power generation capacity.
•	Wind Potential: Phu Yen's coastal location provides potential for both onshore and offshore wind power, and the province is actively calling for investment in new wind projects.
•	Energy Efficiency Programs: The province's electric power company has been commended for its efforts in implementing energy saving and efficiency programs, promoting the use of energy-efficient appliances (like compact fluorescent lamps, solar water heaters) and urging businesses and households to reduce consumption during peak hours (typically 5 PM - 9 PM).
3. Key Challenges and Unresolved Issues
Despite the rapid growth, assessments point to several critical challenges:
•	Grid Overload and Stability: The hot development of numerous self-initiated solar projects has led to overloading the transmission grid infrastructure, creating difficulties in the safe and effective operation of the national power system.
•	Environmental Concerns: The surge in solar power also raises future concerns about the management of industrial waste, particularly the disposal and recycling of large volumes of photovoltaic panels after their operational life (15-20 years).
•	Hydropower Management Conflicts: The operational regulation of interconnected hydropower reservoirs, especially on the Ba River, has been criticized for being ineffective, causing widespread flooding in the downstream areas during the rainy season and water shortages for agricultural production during the dry season.
•	Capacity and Infrastructure Readiness: Assessments of economic zones like Nam Phu Yen indicate that, while natural resources for solar are strong, infrastructure (smart grids, storage) and organizational capacity for a full energy transition remain a key challenge and require targeted investment.

column19: Dentro del Plan Urbano Distrital de San Borja tenemos un item para una Ciudad Sostenible En este documento se presentan los lineamientos generales para alcanzar a ser una ciudad sostenible para el año 2035, priorizando acciones en los cuatro ejes que se han convertido en los pilares de la gestión ambiental del distrito: movilidad, desarrollo urbano, eficiencia energética y gestión local. Luego de realizar un diagnóstico distrital, presenta una visión: Buscamos formar una ciudad moderna que valore su patrimonio, promoviendo la participación de sus ciudadanos, dentro de una ciudad segura y abierta con espacios públicos de calidad, con una emisión baja de carbono; una ciudad jardín que use eficientemente la energía, así como también el agua, utilizando un transporte sostenible no contaminante para una ciudad que recicla. Propuestas ▪ Uno de los espacios más importantes a intervenir es el cruce de las avenidas Javier Prado y Aviación debido a que actualmente separa toda la zona norte del distrito. ▪ Se propone una normativa que busque mantener el área verde original para cada residente del edificio aprovechando todo espacio posible. ▪ Se propone para el 2018 crecer en riego tecnificado del 19% al 40%. Además 11% de las áreas verdes serán regadas con agua residual tratada, eliminando completamente el uso de agua potable. ▪ Recuperación de la ribera del río Surco. ▪ Plan de arborización. ▪ Instalación de contenedores subterráneos para recolección selectiva de residuos. ▪ Instalación de planta de reaprovechamiento de residuos sólidos. ▪ Ampliación “San Borja en bici” y conexión interdistrital con san isidro y surquillo. ▪ Gestión de semaforización inteligente. ▪ Movilidad y espacio - público, Calles - Verdes. ▪ Uso sostenible de la energía, Iluminación Sostenible. 1.1.2.3. Plan de Desarrollo Local Concertado Urbanova Inmobiliaria anunció la inauguración de su planta de cogeneración eléctrica en La Rambla de San Borja, convirtiéndo el establecimiento en el primer centro comercial del Perú en contar con el modelo de cogeneración para su propio consumo de energía eléctrica implementado por EQUANS Perú. La iniciativa de eficiencia energética comprende la instalación de una planta de cogeneración, la implementación de una plataforma de gestión integral de la energía, la automatización de equipos e instalaciones eléctricas, iluminación led inteligente, el cambio de tecnología con equipos a gas natural, una red de paneles solares, entre otros. El sistema tiene como objetivo obtener simultáneamente energía eléctrica para alimentar al centro comercial (iluminación interna, externa y carga de autos eléctricos) y energía térmica para generar aire acondicionado, brindándole al centro comercial cierta independencia, calidad energética, confiabilidad, y una mejor productividad. De esta manera, el proyecto permitirá que La Rambla efectúe una transición sostenible a tecnologías emergentes, debido al consumo de energía eléctrica de origen 100% renovable. Se estima que el Proyecto de Cogeneración Eléctrica evite emisiones de CO2 equivalentes a 610 toneladas anuales. Esta cifra representa la energía usada por aproximadamente 29 viviendas durante un año.
